The dessert meaning is more salient in contemporary usage (e.g. “peach cobbler” as a common dish in AmE, frequent in recipes, media, and everyday speech). The shoemaker sense, while historically primary and still listed first in dictionaries, has become less frequent because the profession itself is rare; speakers more often default to “shoe repair” phrases. Corpus and Google-hit distributions also tilt toward the food sense in recent decades. Therefore an approximate 1:3 split (25 % vs. 75 %) is a reasonable estimate for the first meaning that comes to mind across a mixed group of English speakers.

The isolated word "will" triggers the modal/auxiliary sense first for the large majority of speakers because that use dominates everyday input (far higher token frequency than either nominal sense). The volition sense surfaces next most readily via fixed expressions such as “free will” or “strong will.” The testament/legal sense is the most contextually narrow and therefore least likely to be the first meaning retrieved. The resulting distribution (80 / 15 / 5) sums to 100 and reflects these frequency and accessibility differences.
